W7221000820.abstract: In design applications, simulations enable rapid iterations and adjustments to device architecture, minimizing costs compared to physical prototyping. The simulation of piezoelectric effects for piezoelectric devices has traditionally relied on the Finite Element Method (FEM), known for its accuracy and reliability. As Machine Learning (ML) technologies advance, Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) emerge as alternatives to accelerate these multiphysics simulations, rendering them more flexible and compensating for data scarcity by leveraging physical principles. This study aims to develop a robust PINN architecture for simulation of cantilever beam Energy Harvesting (EH) devices, which in practice may make use of either the indirect or direct piezoelectric effect. The methodology involves designing a tailored PINN architecture integrating piezoelectric governing Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) as loss functions. The model was trained and validated against FEM results. Using PINNs presents several challenges, including modeling coupled physical domains and managing optimization instabilities arising from automatic differentiation of the physics-informed loss function, which makes training more sensitive than in standard supervised learning. Nevertheless, our model successfully simulated the indirect piezoelectric effect, approximating mechanical deflections (in two dimensions) and electric potential to high accuracy (relative L² errors of 1.9596 × 10-1, 1.9291 × 10-1 and 1.0272 × 10-3, respectively). In addition, although FEM data was not available for validation, simulation of the direct piezoelectric effect demonstrated physically consistent results and aligned with expected behavior. The model's performance and accuracy in capturing piezoelectric effects, as well as reliability in simulating complex phenomena, showcases the power of PINNs for industrial applications. PINNs are proven to be a powerful tool for optimizing the design and efficiency of EH systems.

W7221020395.abstract: Diabetes mellitus is a global chronic disease that affects the whole body and not just glucose metabolism. In diabetes, non-invasive ocular changes can help understand microvascular, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory processes. This analysis looks at the eye as a biomarker platform for diabetes-related disease, with retinal imaging informing systemic pathophysiology and the emergence of AI-assisted approaches. With improvements in optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography, it is possible to observe neurovascular changes that can occur before the clinical onset of diabetic retinopathy. Issues in the retina have also been connected to problems with the heart, brain, kidneys, and cognition. However, much of the evidence for problems involving the heart and cognition comes from studies on people without diabetes. Also, most of the available data are observational, rather than coming from controlled studies. As a result, retinal measurements should be considered candidate biomarkers rather than clinically validated predictors or surrogate endpoints for systemic outcomes. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has reached a phase of clinical maturity such that it can be used in the automated screening of diabetic retinopathy. However, it remains investigational for systemic risk prediction, such as for chronic kidney disease, cardiovascular outcomes, and cognitive decline. Equally, the therapeutic implications of retinal neurodegeneration and other imaging biomarkers are under-validated for systemic decisions. Before retinal biomarkers can be used in precision diabetes care, we need more diabetes-specific prospective studies to establish standardized measurements, the clinical meaning of thresholds, incremental predictive value above and beyond established risk factors, reproducibility, cost-effectiveness, and evidence of improved outcomes.

W7221182453.abstract: ABSTRACT Background and Aims Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease with a relapsing course and significant morbidity. In outpatients with moderate‐to‐severe UC assessment of treatment response is often delayed, limiting timely treatment optimisation. Intestinal ultrasonography (IUS) is a noninvasive point‐of‐care modality with high correlation to endoscopic activity. Early changes in bowel wall thickness (BWT) may predict treatment response in hospitalised patients with acute severe UC, but prospective validation in the outpatient setting is lacking. This study aims to evaluate whether early changes in IUS parameters, particularly BWT, can predict treatment response and the need for treatment escalation in outpatients initiating systemic corticosteroids, biologics or small molecules. Methods This is a prospective, nonrandomised, double‐blinded and multicentre study conducted across seven Nordic inflammatory bowel disease centres. Outpatients with moderate‐to‐severe UC extending beyond the rectum, initiating systemic corticosteroids or advanced therapy, will be included. IUS will be performed at baseline and repeated at day 2 ± 1, day 7 ± 1, day 90 ± 14 and at week 52 ± 4 using standardised protocols and evaluated by central reading. Clinical indices, biomarkers, endoscopy and patient‐reported outcomes will be collected and correlated with IUS longitudinally. The primary endpoint is the association between early changes in BWT on days 2 and 7 and treatment escalation at 3 and 12 months. Secondary and exploratory endpoints include remission outcomes, time to response, quality of life and integration of multiomics data. Results Results are pending; recruitment is planned from March 2026 to February 2028. Discussion This multicentre double‐blinded study will prospectively evaluate early IUS as a noninvasive predictor of treatment response in outpatients with moderate‐to‐severe UC. The design enables rapid point‐of‐care assessment of therapeutic efficacy and results will allow for an individualised, dynamic and treat‐to‐target management approach. Key strengths include standardised IUS protocols, blinded evaluations, integration of endoscopic, biochemical and multiomics data, and the creation of an image repository that enables future artificial intelligence applications. Limitations of this study includes the observational design, causal inferences cannot be established and residual confounding may persist despite multivariable adjustment; additionally, treatment heterogeneity, including concomitant corticosteroid use, may complicate interpretation of early imaging changes. Furthermore, exclusion of patients with isolated proctitis and the exploratory nature of the omics analyses may limit generalisability and require external validation. Trial Registration Clinicaltrials.gov. EU CT number: 2026‐527929‐35‐00

W7221355859.abstract: Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have advanced from 3.8% to 27.01% power conversion efficiency (PCE) in 17 years, while their lead-free analogs have reached 17.1%, and perovskite/silicon tandems exceeded 34%. Machine learning (ML) is credited with accelerating much of this progress, yet its evaluation is rarely examined. Here, we report a critical audit of 80 ML-PSC studies from 2024 to 2026. Among these, 89% report no error analysis on any sub-range of PCE, none report nested cross-validation, 48% rely on a single train/test split, and only 9% predict stability over time. Models that appear accurate overall can therefore fail in the sparse high-PCE region, which is the region most relevant to commercialization. We reframe high-PCE prediction as an imbalanced regression problem, establish imbalance-aware techniques, recommend an evaluation workflow, and propose a five-pillar roadmap. Further progress depends as much on shared evaluation and reporting standards as on new algorithms.

W7221578490.abstract: Accurate prediction of the internal states of Lithium-Ion Batteries is critical for the safety and efficiency of Battery Management Systems (BMS), particularly for advanced indicators such as the State of Available Power (SOAP). While physics-based electrochemical models like the Doyle-Fuller-Newman (DFN) or Pseudo-Two-Dimensional (P2D) model offer superior fidelity compared to empirical Equivalent Circuit Models (ECMs), their high computational complexity typically precludes their use in real-time embedded applications, specially when high mesh resolution and multiple model calls within specialized algorithms are needed. This paper proposes a novel approach by using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to generate a Reduced Order Model (ROM) of the battery cell dynamics. By embedding physical equations directly into the neural network loss function, we derive a data-efficient ROM capable of capturing the electrochemical behavior defined by the DFN and Single Particle Model (SPM) framework. This ROM is subsequently integrated into a SOAP estimation algorithm. We demonstrate that the PINN-based approach outperforms classical numerical solvers in terms of execution speed while maintaining a high degree of physical consistency. The results suggest that physics-embedded machine learning provides a viable pathway for implementing nextgeneration, physics-based power prediction algorithms on standard BMS hardware.

W7221759295.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming an integral part of the software development lifecycle, and the capabilities granted to them allow an agent to act with the user's authority on any resource it can access. The reach that gives an agent its utility is equally available to an attacker who can steer it. Anything an agent ingests can carry an injected instruction, and since the model does not reliably distinguish instructions from data, indirect prompt injection should be mitigated by mediating the effects the agent produces. Such mediation faces a structural difficulty. Legitimate work and the first step of an attack often look alike when an individual action is observed, and what separates them lies later in the trace, so a monitor limited to allow and deny is forced to decide before the evidence accumulates. We present Kairos, a reference monitor at the isolation boundary of an unmodified, opaque agent, where a tool call, a shell command, and a script the agent writes all cross the boundary as the same file and network operations, so that confinement holds regardless of the agent's behavior. A declarative policy that states which sources are trusted decides most effects deterministically and defers the rest, which are held while the agent continues speculatively. A decision oracle with bounded authority, such as a language model or a human, releases or refuses each deferred effect on the trace. Across three benchmarks and three agent models, Kairos outperforms existing defenses in the trade-off between attack success and utility. In particular, on AgentDojo, it reduces attack success from 47.0\% to 2.7\% while its benign utility stays at the level of the undefended agent.

W7221790027.abstract: Gifted learners require instructional environments that transcend conventional pedagogical boundaries, offering adaptive challenge, metacognitive scaffolding, and high degrees of learner autonomy. This study presents the design, implementation, and empirical evaluation of the AI-Enhanced Self-Directed Learning (AESDL) framework an integrated adaptive system grounded in Treffinger's Independent Learner Model (ILM) and operationalized through an ensemble of five artificial intelligence (AI) technologies: the Google Gemini API (as central orchestration controller), cognitive computing, multi-agent systems (MAS), expert systems, and automatic speech recognition. The model is built upon four core ILM components Guidance, Self-Development, Enrichment, and Seminars/In-Depth Study each computationally instantiated through dedicated AI subsystems. A quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test control group design was employed with 50 gifted secondary school learners (25 experimental, 25 control) drawn from model gifted-education classrooms in Khartoum State, Sudan. The experimental group received eight weeks of instruction via the AESDL system; the control group received equivalent instruction through conventional electronic resources. Outcome measures self-directed learning skills, problem-solving capacity, and academic enrichment achievement (each scored on a 50-point scale) were analyzed using independent-samples t-tests with Cohen's d effect sizes. Results indicated statistically significant and practically large superiority of the AESDL condition: self-directed learning (t(48) = 7.91, p < .001, d = 2.24), problem-solving (t(48) = 5.52, p < .001, d = 1.56), and academic achievement (t(48) = 6.50, p < .001, d = 1.84). These findings advance the empirical evidence base for AI-mediated gifted education and provide actionable design principles for intelligent adaptive learning systems. The control condition comprised conventional electronic learning resources (digital textbooks, instructional videos, and static online exercises). Ninety-five-percent confidence intervals for the between-group mean differences were [9.13, 15.35], [5.62, 12.06], and [7.02, 13.30] for self-directed learning, problem-solving, and academic achievement, respectively. Given the modest sample (n = 50) and the near-ceiling experimental-group scores, these findings should be interpreted with caution regarding potential ceiling effects and limited external validity, and warrant independent replication with larger, more diverse samples.

W7221792239.abstract: Weight-space learning treats the weights of neural networks as data, processed by other models called metanetworks. A key challenge is that different weights can realize the same function, related by a group of symmetries the metanetwork should respect. While symmetry-aware metanetworks for simple architectures such as MLPs are well developed, a comprehensive treatment of transformers, and in particular transformer-based language models, is still missing. Importantly, their weight space has a richer symmetry group: beyond neuron permutations, attention introduces continuous general-linear symmetries of the attention matrices and permutations of entire heads. Existing methods for transformer weights either capture only part of these symmetries or are restricted to a single, fixed architecture, and none accounts for language-model-specific components such as the token embeddings. Building on graph metanetworks, we propose a graph-based approach that is both symmetry-aware and applicable across depths and widths. We formalize a weight-space symmetry group of complete decoder-only language models and provide a graph construction that is invariant to it. We further introduce two new transformer-population datasets with novel tasks, such as training-corpus prediction and fine-tuning detection, on which our approach notably outperforms existing baselines.

W7222008408.abstract: Many real-world questions demand not a single fact but an organized collection of them, yet existing factual knowledge benchmarks almost exclusively target single answer retrieval. We introduce ListQA, a benchmark of 9,045 human-curated, cross-validated questions (audited error rate of 1.7%) that require LLMs to recall multiple facts and compose them into structured lists of 3-10 elements. Questions range from flat lists ("Which NCAA teams went undefeated between 2000 and 2024?") to hierarchical lists with sub-attributes ("...and what was their record and result?"), spanning eight categories across 60+ countries. An evergreen design (explicit temporal constraints or historically immutable facts) keeps ground truth valid without periodic updates. For evaluation, we frame element matching as a linear sum assignment problem: optimal bipartite matching paired with LLM-based semantic grading jointly captures factual accuracy, hallucination, and format compliance. We benchmark 34 models (8 families, 42 configurations across standard and thinking enabled inference) and find: the best standard-inference model scores below 37% LLM-Judge-F1, multi-faceted questions are harder across the board, and providing the source Wikipedia page lifts scores dramatically, confirming that models can organize facts but struggle to retrieve them from parameters alone. Extended analyses cover base vs. instruction-tuned checkpoints and token efficiency. We release the dataset and evaluation code.

W7222343111.abstract: Long-horizon tasks expose a weakness of monolithic tool-use loops: one agent must decompose, execute, and verify a task within a single trajectory. We introduce LAGO, which treats specialized language agents as reusable temporally extended options. A meta-agent retrieves options from a persistent library or spawns new ones, dispatches sub-tasks, verifies results, and admits successful novel options. The library grows across tasks without updating model weights. On 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks, frozen Qwen3.5-35B-A3B in both roles resolves 58.6% under single-attempt evaluation with the official Docker evaluator. On a fixed 150-task subset, we re-run mini-SWE-agent, Terminus 2, and LAGO with the same policy, temperature, task IDs, and evaluator; their resolve rates are 49.3%, 57.3%, and 60.3%, respectively. Cross-model experiments provide evidence consistent with a role for decomposition quality. A 50-task component ablation finds four fewer resolved tasks without decomposition, two fewer with shuffled reused content, and six fewer without the library. These results support reusable agent-options as a practical abstraction for task streams, while leaving component-level causality task- and model-dependent.

W7222376512.abstract: Autonomous enterprise security governance is becoming essential as organizations increasingly adopt cloud-native architectures, distributed applications, hybrid infrastructures, and multi-cloud environments. Traditional security governance approaches frequently depend on static policies, manual approvals, and reactive threat detection, limiting their ability to respond effectively to dynamic enterprise risks. This research proposes an intelligent security governance framework integrating agentic artificial intelligence (AI) with cloud-native policy orchestration to improve security automation, regulatory compliance, and operational resilience. The framework employs specialized AI agents to continuously monitor infrastructure activities, analyze security events, evaluate policy violations, prioritize risks, and coordinate appropriate mitigation actions. Cloud-native technologies, including container orchestration, policy-as-code, identity management, security monitoring, and automated compliance validation, provide the operational foundation. A centralized governance layer establishes policy consistency, accountability, and controlled authorization across distributed enterprise environments. The proposed methodology combines architectural modeling, simulated enterprise workloads, threat scenarios, policy evaluation, and comparative performance analysis to assess detection accuracy, response latency, compliance coverage, and automation effectiveness. Human oversight, explainable decisions, least-privilege access, and auditable execution are incorporated to reduce unintended autonomous actions. The framework aims to demonstrate how agentic AI can strengthen adaptive governance while maintaining organizational control and regulatory accountability. The research contributes an integrated approach for developing scalable, context-aware, and resilient enterprise security governance systems capable of supporting evolving cloud-native operations and increasingly complex cybersecurity requirements.

W7222382962.abstract: The Large Language Model (LLMs) have proven to be extremely powerful in generating high-quality fluent and informative responses to a wide range of prompts. The main issue with such model is that they tend to generate hallucinated responses i.e. responses that contain information not supported by the context. The issue with detecting hallucinations is that a response might sound reasonable, even if it contains irrelevant or incorrect information. The prior work on the topic has had limited success, as the majority of it focuses on utilizing only one type of evidence to detect hallucination, which might be insufficient to capture the complexity of phenomenon. This paper proposes a novel method for detecting hallucination in LLMs responses that utilize a hybrid of different signals to detect hallucinations. This paper introduces a set of signals based on semantic consistency, semantic uncertainty, factual or contextual verification, prompt sensitivity and model variability that evaluate the responses from different angles to determine whether it contains any hallucinations. The paper tests the model on the HaluEval dataset and compares it to individual signals to see whether the hybrid approach would perform better than any single signal. It evaluates the performance using standard classification evaluation metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and PR-AUC and performs an ablation study to assess the impact of each individual signal. Overall, this paper aims to improve the current understanding of the hallucination detection task and the factors influencing it and provide an effective solution to the problem.

W7222755715.abstract: Recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems build stronger AI systems, is one promising route to superintelligence. We study a weaker form that can be measured today: frontier agents post-training a small raw base model with public data, as a test of their research potential. We build Athanor, an open agent-native system for autonomous post-training research (AutoPostTrain) on real GPUs. We give the agents full research autonomy, low-friction engineering tools, and efficient starter code. The agents carry out the research themselves: they read datasets and evaluation results, build their training data, write and modify training algorithms, tune hyperparameters, and analyze the results to decide what to try next. They work in a sandbox and cannot use external teacher models. Athanor's services supply frozen evaluation, managed jobs, decontaminated data, a persistent research record, and a held-out suite the agents are unaware of. In a 104-hour campaign, a team of four Claude Opus 5.5 agents, each on an eight-GPU node and given no research advice, improves Qwen3-4B-Base from 15.9 to 67.3 on a six-task development suite and from 9.2 to 48.2 on a held-out suite, against 66.5 and 47.9 for the official Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a team of frontier agents can autonomously post-train a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model that matches or surpasses the official instruct version on average. The campaign's full record shows that the agents reach this level by recombining known methods and each other's models: SFT on public reasoning data, RL with a rollout change one agent introduced, weight merges across agents, and rounds of self-distillation. With execution handled, today's agents already have the engineering and research ability to conquer this task. We hope Athanor provides a foundation for scaling autonomous AI research.

W7222883089.abstract: Autonomous artificial intelligence agents extend generative AI from producing content on demand to pursuing goals through planning, memory, tool use, environmental feedback, and iterative action. This shift matters organizationally because agency is no longer confined to recommendation: systems can increasingly initiate and coordinate consequential work. This article integrates research on AI-enabled work, algorithmic management, organizational design, human–AI collaboration, automation, and responsible AI to explain the transition from copilots to digital coworkers. The review distinguishes five configurations—tool, copilot, teammate, delegate, and coworker—and argues that the central organizational variable is not technical capability alone but the allocation of decision authority. We synthesize evidence showing that AI assistance can improve speed and quality in bounded tasks, often benefiting less experienced workers, while also producing uneven performance at the frontier of model capability. Extending this evidence to agentic systems, we develop an authority allocation matrix based on task risk, reversibility, verifiability, and auditability. We identify three mechanisms through which agents reshape organizations: role reconfiguration, authority redistribution, and coordination redesign. Benefits arise when agents compress search and execution costs, diffuse expertise, and enable new forms of modular organizing. Risks arise when action outpaces verification, responsibility becomes diffused, tacit knowledge erodes, or agents acquire excessive access to organizational resources. We propose a layered governance architecture combining explicit mandates, least-privilege access, execution limits, provenance, continuous monitoring, and human escalation rights. The article concludes with propositions and a research agenda for studying agentic organizing through field experiments, longitudinal process research, digital trace analysis, and comparative institutional designs.

W7222983945.abstract: Recent studies have shown that position bias remains a critical vulnerability in large language models (LLMs), undermining both the integrity of multiple-choice evaluations and the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation. However, existing understanding of this phenomenon is largely derived from studies with limited model coverage and English-centric benchmarks, leaving the behavior of frontier models and diverse languages underexplored. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation of position bias across model scales ranging from billion-level to trillion-level parameters, covering both multiple-choice and multi-document tasks in five languages. Our experiments reveal that while position bias remains noticeable in small-scale models and Non-English languages, increasing model scale and employing standard Chain-of-Thought prompting significantly mitigate this issue. Moreover, we demonstrate that emerging \emph{thinking models} with extended reasoning capabilities are nearly immune to position bias, suggesting a costly but general approach toward resolving this vulnerability.

W7222998051.abstract: Dental image segmentation is an important problem in oral diagnosis and treatment planning due to the high demand for accurate localization and boundary definition.Deep Learning (DL) techniques have dramatically enhanced the ability and accuracy of segmentation tasks in many clinical domains, especially in recent years. Transformer-based architectures were initially designed for natural language processing but have recently also been used within computer vision and medical imaging with comparable success. Between these hybrid approaches, both convolutional and transformer based methods have achieved remarkable productivity improvements for semantic segmentation. This article proposes one possible way to predict which architecture is the most efficient for pixel-wise segmentation using iVisionLab data, based on high-performance deep learning architectures. The transformer-augmented VIT SwinUNETR++ delivered the best F1-Score (95.96%), precision (95.95%), and recall (95.96%). These results demonstrate not only balanced prediction performance, but also better generalization quality than the other three models DeepLab V3+, R2UNet, and SegFormer-B0 evaluated. In addition, the large predictive ability of VIT SwinUNETR++ demonstrates that it is an attractive model for high-performance high-complexity medical image analysis.

W7223019623.abstract: Context: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) is rapidly emerging as a major research paradigm in which artificial intelligence systems move beyond response generation toward autonomous, goal-directed reasoning, planning, tool use, memory, adaptation, and multi-agent collaboration. The rapid expansion and disciplinary fragmentation of this literature create a need for systematic mapping of its research landscape. Aim: This study maps the global development, scholarly influence, geographical distribution, and collaboration patterns of Agentic AI research during 2023–2026. Approach: A bibliometric and science-mapping analysis was conducted using Scopus publications retrieved on 1 July 2026. Following systematic screening and duplicate removal, 3,425 publications were analyzed using Biblioshiny. Key Findings: Agentic AI exhibited an annual growth rate of 215.04%, with 9,166 authors contributing across 1,015 sources. Conference papers dominated the corpus (2,654), reflecting the field’s rapidly evolving technological character. China and the United States were the leading corresponding-author countries, while Tsinghua University was the most productive affiliation. Citation analysis identified several highly influential foundational studies. Interpretation: The findings indicate that Agentic AI is developing rapidly into a distinct, collaborative, and increasingly established research domain centered on autonomous and coordinated AI systems. Contribution: This study provides a broad Scopus-based quantitative map of contemporary Agentic AI scholarship and identifies emerging priorities for evaluation, multi-agent coordination, security, explainability, human–AI collaboration, and governance.

W7223065090.abstract: The increasing use of data-driven technologies has created significant opportunities for intelligent computing, predictive analytics, and automated decision-making. However, conventional machine learning approaches often require centralized data collection, which can introduce privacy risks, security vulnerabilities, and regulatory challenges. Federated learning has emerged as an alternative approach that enables multiple devices or organizations to collaboratively train machine learning models without routinely transferring their raw training data to a central server. Instead, participating clients perform local training and communicate model updates to a coordinating server or aggregation mechanism. This approach can reduce direct data sharing and support collaborative learning across distributed environments. This paper presents a review of federated learning, focusing on its fundamental architecture, training process, aggregation techniques, applications, and technical limitations. It examines the role of federated learning in healthcare, financial services, mobile computing, industrial systems, and smart environments. The paper also discusses challenges involving communication overhead, statistical heterogeneity, device limitations, malicious participants, privacy leakage, and model convergence. Furthermore, it explores complementary techniques, including differential privacy, secure aggregation, and homomorphic encryption, that can strengthen the protection of information during collaborative training. Finally, future research directions are identified in adaptive aggregation, communication-efficient optimization, cross-silo collaboration, edge intelligence, and trustworthy model evaluation. The review concludes that federated learning offers a promising framework for distributed machine learning, but its privacy and performance benefits depend on the system architecture, threat model, data distribution, and security mechanisms employed.

W7223113217.abstract: Firms that sell to other firms on credit now face a new design choice. Software agents built on large language models can gather evidence, draft credit memos, release held orders and chase overdue invoices. Yet there is little guidance on how much of this work an agent should do without a person. Most research on artificial intelligence in credit asks how accurate a model is, and most of it studies consumer lending. It says little about the decision rights of autonomous agents in business-to-business trade credit, where much activity sits outside consumer-protection and bank model-risk rules. This conceptual paper addresses that gap. It integrates research on trade credit, credit scoring, language-model agents, levels of automation, agency theory and model-risk governance. From this synthesis it builds the Verifiability-Weighted Autonomy framework. The central claim is simple: the autonomy granted to an agent should rise with the verifiability of the evidence behind a decision and fall with the decision's financial exposure and irreversibility. The paper defines four autonomy tiers and a transparent allocation rule. It maps twelve common trade-credit decisions onto the tiers. It proposes a Propose–Verify–Dispose architecture in which language-model agents propose, deterministic checks verify, and policy rules or people dispose. It offers seven testable propositions and four measures for future empirical work. For managers, the framework turns a vague question, "can we trust the agent?", into a concrete design rule that fits existing delegation-of-authority practice. Keywords: large language model agents; trade credit; delegation of authority; model risk management; human oversight

W7223181773.abstract: High-density and high-areal-density plasmas are the fundamental prerequisites for fusion ignition in inertial confinement fusion. To generate such plasma conditions via the double-cone ignition (DCI) scheme, a laser facility delivering 160 kJ nanosecond laser pulses is currently under construction in Shanghai. In this work, we propose a compression-stage optimization method for colliding plasmas that integrates two-dimensional radiation hydrodynamics simulations with a genetic algorithm (GA). We show that an isochoric colliding plasma with a peak density of 409 g/cm3 and an areal density of 1.63 g/cm2 can be achieved. We also identify an optimal implosion velocity range of about 251–283 km/s for the plasma jet-collision process for this 160 kJ facility, which can be described by a physically interpretable fit curve. To enable large-scale, high-fidelity predictions of colliding plasma behavior, we develop a neural network ensemble surrogate model trained on over 20 000 simulation datasets derived from the aforementioned GA optimization. This surrogate model takes laser pulse shapes and target geometric parameters as inputs to predict the key plasma parameters, including peak density, areal density, and implosion velocity. The model achieves predictions with an average relative error below 3% and accelerates the optimization process by more than two orders of magnitude compared to direct MULTI-2D simulations. This work establishes a solid foundation for the rapid design and parameter optimization of future DCI experiments.

W7223219224.abstract: Masked diffusion language models have emerged as an alternative to autoregressive models, enabling parallel token generation. However, standard masked diffusion language models use a shared noise schedule across positions without explicitly encoding which positions should be resolved first. Many tasks exhibit a natural priority among positions: document titles and section headings can guide the generation of body text, while Sudoku cells determined directly from the initial clues can help resolve more difficult cells. To incorporate this notion of priority (or hierarchy) among token positions, we introduce the Hierarchical Masked Diffusion Language Model (HMDLM), which augments each token position with a hierarchy level available as part of the training data, and requires zero or minimal additional annotations. It factors generation into two passes: the first predicts a hierarchy distribution over masked positions, the second predicts token distributions conditioned on it. Giving each hierarchy level its own noise schedule induces a soft, controllable preference for revealing higher-priority positions earlier while keeping decoding fully parallel. Our formulation is mathematically grounded, and we re-derive the forward and reverse processes and the NELBO for this factorization. Our evaluation shows that for the task of language generation on LM1B, HMDLM reduces perplexity by more than 1.5 points over Anchored Diffusion Language Model (ADLM), a recently proposed strong diffusion baseline; on WikiHow, we see a drop in perplexity of up to 4.4 pts on ADLM and up to 7 pts against MDLM. An LLM judge on WikiHow prefers HMDLM generations (the two variants combined) more than $2\times$ as often as the baseline. On the task of solving Sudoku puzzles requiring multi-step reasoning, it improves solution accuracy by up to $8.6\%$ absolute points over existing diffusion baselines.

W7223456774.abstract: Abstract Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) continues to pose a serious threat to global public health, with African healthcare systems carrying a disproportionate burden. Although antimicrobial stewardship programs have been recommended as an important strategy for improving antimicrobial use and slowing the emergence of resistance, implementation across many African healthcare systems continues to face several challenges, including workforce shortages, weak laboratory infrastructure, and poor surveillance systems. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have shown promising potential in strengthening antimicrobial stewardship through clinical decision support, resistance prediction, automated surveillance, and data extraction from weak health information systems. However, the application of AI in antimicrobial stewardship across Africa is still at an early stage, with most systems remaining at pilot or research stages. This commentary discusses current opportunities, examines major barriers affecting implementation, and proposes recommendations that may support sustainable integration of AI into antimicrobial stewardship programs across Africa.

W7223462872.abstract: Cancer immunotherapy has fundamentally reshaped oncology by demonstrating that immune modulation can generate durable clinical responses in patients with advanced malignancies. However, the effectiveness of current immunotherapeutic approaches remains restricted by substantial interpatient variability, primary resistance, and acquired immune escape mechanisms. These limitations largely originate from the complexity of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), where malignant cells interact dynamically with heterogeneous immune populations, stromal components, metabolic networks, and molecular signaling pathways. Conventional biomarker approaches based on individual immune markers, such as PD-L1 expression or tumor mutational burden, provide incomplete predictions because they fail to capture the multidimensional nature of tumor immune interactions. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative approach capable of integrating large-scale biological datasets generated through genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, single-cell sequencing, and spatial omics technologies. Machine learning, deep learning, and emerging foundation models provide unprecedented opportunities to decode immune ecosystems, identify novel biomarkers, predict immunotherapy responsiveness, and accelerate the development of personalized cancer treatments. Recent advances demonstrate that AI-driven models can characterize immune cell states, reconstruct spatial immune architectures, and improve patient stratification for immune checkpoint inhibitors. This review discusses the evolving intersection between AI and cancer immunology, focusing on how computational approaches are transforming TIME analysis, biomarker discovery, and precision immunotherapy. We critically evaluate current challenges, including algorithmic bias, model interpretability, clinical validation, and regulatory implementation. Finally, we highlight future directions toward AI-powered immuno-oncology platforms capable of integrating biological knowledge with computational intelligence to achieve individualized and more effective cancer therapies.

W7223655785.abstract: Abstract This theoretical article examines artificial intelligence in organizational digitalization. It distinguishes digitization, digitalization, and digital transformation, then combines sociotechnical theory with the dynamic capabilities perspective to explain how technology interacts with employees, routines, organizational structures and adaptation. The framework proposes that artificial intelligence supports transformation when aligned with strategy, integrated into processes and complemented by employee expertise, data and responsible governance. It highlights tensions involving discretion, bias, accountability and the fit between standardized systems and local practices. The article contributes propositions for empirical research and argues that AI’s value depends on integrating technical systems with human capabilities and organizational oversight. AI applications can automate repetitive tasks, analyze large amounts of data, personalize services and support decisions. However, their effects depend on data quality, employee skills, leadership commitment and the organizational context. For this reason, the article moves the focus beyond the simple adoption of AI and highlights the organizational capabilities and governance needed to integrate it responsibly. Keywords: artificial intelligence; organizational digitalization; digital transformation; dynamic capabilities; sociotechnical systems; AI adoption; responsible AI governance.

W7223997417.abstract: Abstract Extracellular vesicles (EVs), including those commonly described as exosomes, carry proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids that reflect the molecular state of their parent cells, making them attractive biomarkers for liquid biopsy-based cancer diagnosis. Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS), which builds on conventional Raman spectroscopy (RS), can read this cargo as vibrational fingerprints, label-free or via targeted nanoprobes, with high sensitivity from small sample volumes. This review examines recent advances in SERS-based exosome/EV analysis for cancer diagnosis, following the workflow from sample to diagnostic decision. We discuss how EV isolation, characterization, heterogeneity, and coisolated lipoproteins and proteins shape the measured spectra and review plasmonic substrates, biosensor and microfluidic platforms, label-free versus label-based strategies, and Raman band assignments. Particular emphasis is placed on artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) for decoding exosome/EV SERS fingerprints, from conventional classifiers to deep learning (DL) and explainable AI, together with common pitfalls such as small cohorts, spectrum-level data leakage, class imbalance, and a lack of external validation. Applications in cancer detection, classification, subtyping, and monitoring are summarized for prostate, lung, breast, and pancreatic cancers, and representative platforms are compared by analytical performance and clinical readiness and against circulating tumor DNA and circulating tumor cell assays. Finally, we offer perspectives on the standardization, reference materials, shared spectral databases, and multicenter validation needed for clinical translation, positioning AI/ML-assisted SERS as a complementary tool for cancer triage and monitoring.

W7224051465.abstract: Wave propagation, governed by partial differential equations (PDEs), plays a critical role in structural health monitoring (SHM). However, traditional numerical solvers suffer from discretization errors, heavy meshing requirements, and prohibitive computational costs in large or high-frequency domains. Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) offers an alternative by embedding physics into neural architectures, reducing reliance on dense data and ensuring physically consistent solutions. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) exemplify this approach but often fail to capture the discontinuities and sharp gradients of hyperbolic wave equations owing to spectral bias and optimization instability. This thesis introduces SciNoNet, a multi-head PINN that predicts the wavefield by decomposing it into three outputs: wave potential, coefficient, and exponent of the wavefield displacement. This design improves training stability and enables accurate learning of high-frequency guided wave patterns beyond the capability of classical PINNs. In this study, both soft constraints (PDE terms in the loss) and hard constraints (PDE terms embedded in neural network architecture) are explored along with different task typologies (regression or classification). SciNoNet successfully reconstructed the wavefield with high fidelity, even when trained on just 0.25% of labeled data. A custom empirical loss function further improved accuracy, outperforming existing baseline loss formulations. Overall, SciNoNet with the custom adaptive loss function demonstrates a significant advancement in guided wave modeling, combining physics-informed learning with multi-task neural networks to achieve efficient, interpretable wavefield predictions.

W7224111489.abstract: The primordial sound waves in the baryon-photon plasma are imprinted on the large-scale galaxy distribution as Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO), serving as a cosmological standard ruler to constrain dark energy and the Hubble parameter. The upcoming 21cm intensity-mapping arrays are designed to map the 21cm emission across large volumes and measure the BAO scale. However, radio interferometers suffer from instrumental systematics that can hinder detection of the cosmological 21cm signal by leaking bright foregrounds into the signal-dominated modes. This work aims to demonstrate that a self-supervised model can predict the instrument systematic state (here, the amplitude of a spectral ripple in the beam width) in interferometric visibilities and potentially disentangle the instrument from the sky without a forward model. Based on the fact that an instrument stays the same as the sky rotates in a drift-scan observation, and that the same sky is observed under different instrument states, we train a convolutional autoencoder to compress the information in the simulated visibilities and separate this information into instrument-only and sky-only latent vectors. The result shows excellent prediction of the unknown instrument systematic for 15 held-out instrument states with $R^2 = 0.9975$ with a linear probe, against $R^2 = -3.55$ for a random-encoder baseline. The instrument-latent carries no detectable sky signal, as measured with a total-power sky proxy, for any held-out test data. The sky-latent vector and instrument-latent vector show partial separation but not complete disentanglement, identifying sky-latent purity as the primary open problem. The results show the ability of the model to recognize the systematic and show a promising path towards an ML-based foreground cleaning pipeline. Full instrument-sky disentanglement constitutes the natural next step.

W7224116462.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for abstractive summarization, yet most prior work in evidence synthesis limits summarization to titles and abstracts and primarily focuses on domains with well-structured reporting formats. These limitations restrict the applicability of automated PICO summarization in social science research, where key information is often embedded in unstructured full-text sections. This study presents a comprehensive end-to-end workflow for fine-tuning LLMs for PICO-oriented summarization of long-form scientific texts in the mental health domain. The proposed pipeline integrates document-level annotation, label-specific instance construction, section-aware data augmentation, long-context model architectures, optimization strategies, and multi-metric evaluation within a unified framework. To systematically examine the effects of model and training choices, we employ a 2×3×3 factorial design varying model architecture, batch size, and learning rate. Performance is evaluated using three complementary metrics (ROUGE, perplexity, MAUVE), supplemented by qualitative comparisons between model-generated and human-written summaries. Results show that LongT5 consistently achieves higher ROUGE and lower perplexity, while BioBART attains higher MAUVE. Across configurations, intermediate learning rates and moderate batch sizes yield the most balanced performance. Further analysis reveals that higher learning rates disproportionately benefit structured and quantitative categories, while gains are more limited for descriptive categories. These findings highlight systematic trade-offs between accuracy, confidence, and diversity in generated summaries. Overall, the proposed pipeline provides practical, evidence-based guidance for applying generative models in long-document evidence synthesis and offers a foundation for future research on finetuning LLMs.

W7224118730.abstract: Machine learning models need large, representative, labeled datasets, but real data are often scarce, imbalanced, costly to label, or restricted by privacy rules. Generative AI can produce synthetic data that keeps the statistical structure of a source dataset without reusing its records, although memorization remains a risk. This paper reviews four generator families: generative adversarial networks, variational autoencoders, diffusion models, and language-model-based tabular generators. It organizes evaluation along three axes: fidelity to real data, downstream utility for model training, and privacy leakage. A worked example shows how synthetic minority samples can rebalance a skewed dataset. The paper then proposes an evaluation protocol that combines train-on-synthetic, test-on-real experiments, differential-privacy accounting, and membership-inference testing. No measured performance result is claimed. The contribution is a structured comparison and an evaluation plan for researchers and practitioners.

W7224248785.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference is computationally intensive, yet the extent to which the interaction language affects energy consumption remains insufficiently understood.This study investigates whether inference energy consumption varies across six European languages: Polish, English, German, French, Spanish, and Russian.Three open-weight models, Llama3.1-8b,Gemma-3-12b, and Qwen2.5-14b, were evaluated using ten semantically equivalent prompts, each translated into the six languages and repeated three times.Experiments were conducted on a workstation-class server equipped with an AMD Radeon RX 7900 XT GPU and the Ollama inference framework.Whole-system power consumption was measured using a calibrated HIOKI PW3337 power meter, and energy efficiency was expressed as energy per generated token (EPT).Mean EPT varied substantially among models: Llama3.1-8bconsumed 6.43 J/token, Qwen2.5-14b10.23 J/token, and Gemma-3-12b 10.87 J/token.Kruskal-Wallis tests identified statistically significant between-language differences only for Llama3.1-8b;no significant differences were found for Qwen2.5-14b or Gemma-3-12b.However, regression analysis for Llama3.1-8bshowed that response length was the dominant predictor of EPT, as fixed inference overhead was amortized over longer outputs.The findings indicate that apparent language-dependent differences in inference energy are driven primarily by generated-output length rather than by language itself.Energy efficiency also depends strongly on model architecture, tokenizer behavior, and inference implementation, highlighting the importance of responselength control and whole-system measurement in Green AI benchmarking.

W7224362251.abstract: The development of Large Language Models has primarily focused on English-centric or massively multilingual paradigms.As a result, the dynamics of mixing just two languages from the very beginning of training remain underexplored, especially for smaller models with limited capacity.In this study, we conduct a controlled set of experiments to evaluate the impact of bilingual corpus during from-scratch pretraining.Using a capacity-constrained Gemma-4-derived 181M-parameter architecture trained on a 10 billion token budget, we compare a purely Turkish baseline against mixtures containing 10%, 20%, or 30% of an auxiliary language.We test four languages to isolate different linguistic relationships: English (a global bridge language), Azerbaijani (closely related sibling), Finnish (morphological peer), and French (lexical pivot).We show that adding any secondary language costs the model fluency on structurally uniform text (academic writing), a capacity tax that grows with the percentage of auxiliary language.Conversely, every mixture lowers perplexity on stylistically divergent text (creative and literary writing).At matched mixture ratios Azerbaijani yields the lowest perplexity on creative and literary text, ahead of the other auxiliary languages.

W7224613247.abstract: Backpack language model embeddings represent each word as a weighted sum of sense vectors, offering more interpretable and intervenable lexical representations than standard contextual embeddings.Backpack sense vector representations show strong performance on lexical similarity tasks in a monolingual setting, as well as cross-lingual transfer through finetuning on aligned parallel multilingual data.Our work investigates whether representations from Backpack models trained from scratch on parallel aligned multilingual data allow for interpretable control without sacrificing translational and cross-lingual representation learning ability.We train matched 131M parameter Transformer and 132M parameter Backpack models from scratch on parallel aligned English-French EuroParl and evaluate their expressivity using validation perplexity, their learned monolingual and cross-lingual lexical relationships using Multi-SimLex and their translational ability using sentence-level cosine similarity.While the Transformer attains higher English and cross-lingual Multi-SimLex, the Backpack outperforms the Transformer on French Multi-SimLex and shows stronger translated-vs-random sentence separation.We finally compare sense-level gender bias ablations on the Backpack model with nullspace projection debiasing on the Transformer, demonstrating the effectiveness of sense vector control for debiasing multilingual representations.

W7224626108.abstract: Thalassemia is one of the most heterogeneous diseases, with more than a thousand mutation types recorded worldwide. Molecular diagnosis of thalassemia by conventional PCR-based DNA analysis is time- and resource-consuming owing to the phenotype variability, disease complexity, and molecular diagnostic test limitations. Thalassemia diagnosis relies heavily on complex interactions among hematological biomarkers, making it challenging to distinguish causal relationships from mere statistical correlations. To address this limitation, this study proposes a causal machine learning framework that integrates causal discovery and counterfactual inference to identify biomarker-driven treatment effects for thalassemia diagnosis. The proposed approach models clinical variables using a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) to capture underlying causal dependencies and enables robust estimation of treatment effects while accounting for confounding factors. To address the primary objective from complementary causal perspectives, the framework combines adjusted regression for confounding control, inverse probability weighting for propensity-based estimation, Random Forest-based analysis for nonlinear feature importance and heterogeneous treatment effects, and bootstrap resampling for uncertainty quantification. The adjusted linear regression model yielded a conservative causal effect estimate of 0.3008, while propensity-based methods demonstrated stronger effects, with IPW producing an estimate of 1.0604. The bootstrap approach confirmed the stability of these findings with a 95% confidence interval of [0.8806, 1.2161], indicating statistically significant treatment influence. Furthermore, heterogeneous effect analysis using CATE revealed substantial variability across individuals, with estimates ranging between 0.0848 and 2.5200, highlighting the importance of personalized assessment. Stratified analysis across age groups showed distinct differences, with the highest effect observed in adolescents (1.3484) and lower effects in children (0.8856), emphasizing demographic-specific variations. The results demonstrate that key biomarkers, particularly hemoglobin-related features, exert significant causal influence on thalassemia diagnosis.

W7224862996.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has moved far beyond what used to be considered as automation. With the growth of Large Language Models (LLMs) in recent years, the systems are no longer just tools that follow instructions of humans, but they are now starting to think, plan, and make sense of the changing situations. Older approaches like the Workflow Management Systems (WMS) and Robotic Process Automation (RPA) still depend on some fixed rules that help in decision-making. They work well for the simple, structured tasks that do not come across dynamic scenarios, but once reasoning, flexibility, or understanding of context is required, they fall short. The rise of Agentic AI technologies change this picture. It introduces systems that have the ability to be autonomous, have a memory, and a sense of goal. It introduces agents that can learn, adapt, and cooperate. This paper reviews how such intelligent agents are being used to create unified workflow automation in corporate communication. It looks at how LLM-based agents can build and adjust workflows dynamically, plan together, and handle real-time coordination that older systems couldn’t manage. Some different frameworks have been discussed in this paper, such as Flow and AgentFlow for modular workflow design, and agentic systems like APA and PROAGENT. The paper also examines some practical tools, including Automatic Meeting Minutes Generation and LLM-based Smart Reply, which show how language understanding can improve collaboration and reduce manual effort in organizations. Along with these technological developments, the review also reflects on the human side of agentic technology. It questions about control, fairness, and how to measure success when our innovations begin to act with a degree of independence. In its essence, it captures the shift from the older rigid automation systems to the more adaptive and self-improving systems that work with people rather than simply for them.

W7225064970.abstract: Abstract Background Synthetic clinical records and narratives can support research and information-system testing without routine access to identifiable patient files. A reusable generator must coordinate record relationships, encounter context, and configurable documentation conventions. Fluent prose and relational consistency alone do not establish clinical fidelity, privacy protection, or reliable training labels. Objective To describe a configurable framework for linked synthetic clinical records and unstructured notes, evaluate the integrity of archived outputs, and verify reference functions for reproducibility and annotation. We also specify an extension toward a virtual electronic health record and continual, on-demand corpus generation. Methods Five stages construct patient anchors, encounters, operational events, demographics, and coverage-guided clinical notes. We examined an archived census of structured exports and two disjoint narrative sets, reproduced isolated implementation fixtures, and tested deterministic seeds, bounded timing, export checks, exact span compilation, and patient-level partitioning in a separate reference module. Python notebooks combine structured sampling with four-bit MedGemma inference. The author-reported generation environment used virtual machines with dual-GPU cloud accelerators. Historical outputs and revised software were evaluated separately; system extensions are presented as proposals. Results The archived census recorded 50,000 patients, 3,225,625 unique encounters, and 375,000 operational events covering 250,000 visits. All sampled encounter counts agreed with patient anchors, and operational patient-visit mappings were valid. The 300 narrative documents represented 250 patients and visits. Strict encounter ordering held, although 341 intervals were shorter than 60 seconds. In the 200-document narrative set, 175 texts contained Markdown fences and 30 contained standalone missing-value tokens. All 39 reference-module tests passed, including 1,000 constructed timing cases. This establishes selected software contracts; no new language-model corpus, clinical assessment, or trained de-identification benchmark was produced. Conclusions Explicit record contracts and coverage planning provide a reusable basis for synthetic clinical data generation. The evidence establishes selected structural properties and bounded software behaviors in one evaluated configuration. The architecture could supply a virtual EHR and repeated narrative releases, but clinical fidelity, sustained operation, privacy risk, and transfer to other settings require independent evaluation.

W7225079366.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) agents carry out longer chains of tasks, oversight must establish whether their behavior still serves an authorized goal. Here, we introduce the anchor: the point at which reference information and human-authorized standards enter an autonomous system. We argue that oversight design should first identify the reference needed to assess goal drift and whether the system's internal record can supply it, then decide who checks and how often, and finally specify who may revise the goal. Goal drift can be impossible to certify from a system's internal record. The missing reference must come from outside that record. Combining a reliability model of checkpoint spacing with evidence from training, execution, and multi-agent coordination, we develop a task taxonomy to guide anchor placement and decisions about which checks to automate. For AI systems that serve human purposes, human judgment is an ineliminable structural requirement in authorizing and revising the purposes and standards that govern autonomous operation, even when routine checking and execution are automated.

W7225107055.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is common among individuals with severe obesity.Metabolic-bariatric surgery improves steatosis and steatohepatitis and is associated with fibrosis regression in many patients; however, hepatic response is heterogeneous, and long-term biopsy data remain limited.This review examines metabolic-bariatric surgery in MASLD from a precision-medicine perspective, focusing on which patients derive hepatic benefit, the magnitude of that benefit, and its durability.We synthesize evidence on clinical stage, non-invasive tests, weight and diabetes trajectories, adipokines, genetics, the gut-liver and thyroid-liver axes, multi-omics, and artificial intelligence.Most proposed predictors reflect baseline disease severity or biological plausibility rather than validated surgery-specific prediction.We therefore present a tiered predict-personalize-monitor framework as a hypothesis-generating research model rather than a clinical algorithm.Routine variables and basic non-invasive tests comprise the essential tier; elastography and magnetic resonance methods are optional advanced tools; genetics, multi-omics, and machine learning remain research tools.Prospective external validation is required before this framework can inform individual treatment allocation or postoperative pharmacotherapy.

W7225114577.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Small Language Models (SLMs) as autonomous agents at the network edge marks a shift in cyber–physical systems and the Internet of Things (IoT). Deploying these non-deterministic reasoning engines in resource-constrained environments, however, disrupts traditional security paradigms. This survey reviews the threats to autonomous edge agents and their defenses. Through a layered taxonomy spanning the Perception, Cognition, Actuation, and Collaboration layers, we categorize the emerging cyber–physical threats, among them sensor-borne prompt injection, context-sequential injection, tool hijacking, and Sybil-based poisoning of the federated substrate. Several have been demonstrated on physical platforms, most starkly the jailbreaking of a deployed commercial robot, whereas the surveyed multi-agent attacks run only in simulation and software; attacks on quantized vision models further show that the aggressive quantization that edge hardware demands can open evasion vectors of its own. Evaluating the prevailing defenses, we expose the latency cost of inference-heavy semantic guardrails and the sequential blindness of stateless pre-execution firewalls, and we map their coverage against the taxonomy, separating experimental from inferred mappings. We flag stateful behavioral tracking as a largely unrefereed direction against the reasoning-to-action gap, not as a settled defense family. The survey’s principal output is a coverage map isolating three edge-induced threats that no edge-deployable runtime mechanism surveyed addresses: energy-targeted resource exhaustion, quantization-specific evasion, and model provenance against supply-chain weight poisoning. For the second, every surveyed hardening strategy that preserves adversarial robustness through quantization has been evaluated only on vision classifiers.

W7225121031.abstract: ABSTRACT The growth of e‐commerce and the corresponding increase in the number of online reviews have driven the demand for recommender systems that capture user preferences. Online reviews contain detailed evaluations of item aspects, and recent studies have employed aspect‐based sentiment analysis (ABSA) to incorporate fine‐grained user sentiment for improved personalisation. However, existing ABSA‐based recommendation approaches rely on predefined aspect categories, which prevents them from capturing user preferences for specific aspect terms and limits their generalisation across diverse domains. To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel ABSA‐based recommendation framework, domain‐agnostic aspect‐aware recommendation (DAAR), which leverages large language models (LLMs) to extract aspect terms and integrate them with sentiment information. First, aspect terms that represent the targets of user evaluation are extracted from review texts using LLMs. Then, semantic representations of the aspect terms are generated using Phrase‐BERT based on bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT), and sentiment scores for each aspect term are obtained through a sentiment analysis model based on decoding‐enhanced BERT with disentangled attention (DeBERTa). Finally, the two representations are combined into a unified representation, and an attention mechanism is applied to capture the relative importance among aspect terms. The resulting representation is then integrated with user–item interactions to predict the final rating. Experimental results on the Yelp and Amazon review datasets demonstrate that DAAR outperforms the baseline models and shows strong generalisation capabilities. This indicates that the proposed framework alleviates domain dependency and more precisely captures user preferences by integrating users' sentiment towards aspect terms.

W7225178640.abstract: Intelligent smart cities require decentralized, transparent, adaptable, and sustainable mechanisms for managing heterogeneous urban systems while preserving data privacy. Traditional centralized approaches face limitations related to privacy, scalability, communication overhead, interpretability, and dependence on centralized infrastructure. This study presents an integrated urban intelligence architecture that combines domain-specific learning, multi-agent artificial intelligence, explainable digital twins, and autonomous decision-making within a unified framework. Each urban domain trains its own model locally, retaining its domain-specific feature representation and prediction objective, while multi-agent intelligence supports coordinated reasoning across transportation, energy, environmental monitoring, and public safety. Explainable digital twins represent urban states, evaluate candidate actions, and provide interpretable evidence for decision-making. The framework follows a continuous Learning → Reasoning → Simulation → Explanation → Decision → Feedback workflow. Experimental evaluation across four domain-specific clients achieves an overall F1-score of 94.79%, decision success rate of 95.3%, autonomous decision rate of 92.8%, and explanation availability of 96.4%. These results demonstrate the integrated capability of distributed learning, collaborative reasoning, contextual simulation, explainability, and autonomous decision support within unified smart-city intelligence architecture.

W7225182313.abstract: Large language model (LLM) based multi-agent systems are rapidly migrating from laboratory prototypes to production deployments in finance, scientific research, industrial digital twins, and urban scheduling. As deployment scales, however, a family of systemic pathologies persists: decision oscillation driven by zero-sum agent interactions, cascade propagation of hallucinated content, long-horizon behavioral drift, value misalignment, and unresolved inter-agent conflict. Existing orchestration paradigms, which rely on instruction dispatch, greedy optimization, or static rules, address only shallow coordination and provide no principled mechanism for convergence. This paper proposes the Recursive Adversarial Engine (RAE), a runtime architecture for multi-agent systems organized around three propositions: bounded adversarial interaction supplies the error-detection signal, recursive correction supplies the error-elimination mechanism, and dynamic checks and balances supply the stability guarantee. We specify a four-layer reference architecture comprising adversarial verification, recursive correction, checks-and-balances scheduling, and steady-state output, and we characterize its convergence behavior through a Lyapunov-style stability argument. A qualitative comparison with self-play, multi-agent debate, alignment, and consensus frameworks delineates the paradigm difference. Engineering implications for high-stakes domains, long-horizon robustness, auditability, and middleware integration are analyzed, and open challenges are identified.

W7225260321.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death in the United States and disproportionately affects racial/ethnic minoritized populations, low-income communities, older adults, and rural residents. Behavioral interventions can reduce cardiovascular risk, yet traditional programs face scalability barriers, including high costs and limited reach. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on the efficacy and equity of patient-directed AI tools that support health education and behavior change for cardiovascular health. Using PRISMA-ScR elements, we searched 10 databases (January 2010 to December 2025), yielding 19 empirical studies evaluating Generation 2.0 AI systems aligned with the American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 (LE8) framework. Of these, five were randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and 14 were nonrandomized (quasi-experimental, observational, or early-stage) studies. AI-enabled interventions such as conversational agents, machine-learning models, and reinforcement-learning systems addressed hypertension, diabetes, heart failure, and related conditions. Among the RCTs, one demonstrated superiority of an AI-powered program over usual care (AI-delivered Diabetes Prevention Program), whereas the remaining four reported outcomes equivalent or non-inferior to standard behavioral care. Effects were most apparent in high-intensity interventions that paired machine learning-based personalization with structured behavioral curricula, although the multi-component nature of these programs limits inference about AI-specific contributions. Across nonrandomized studies, greater engagement intensity was consistently associated with improved cardiometabolic outcomes, although causal attribution to AI-specific mechanisms remains limited. Most studies had small samples, short follow-up, and limited reporting on safety and equity. Technology-intensive interventions were concentrated in higher-resourced settings, and populations with limited health literacy showed reduced engagement. Overall, evidence supports cautious optimism that AI can meaningfully scale personalized cardiovascular prevention; however, realizing that equitable and clinically meaningful impact will require rigorous trials with longer follow-up, explicit behavioral science integration, safety-conscious governance, and equity-centered strategies addressing digital determinants of health.

W7225292194.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive and heterogeneous subtype of breast cancer with limited targeted therapies and poor prognosis. Recent advances in digital pathology and artificial intelligence (AI) are transforming traditional, qualitative histopathology into quantitative, data-driven analysis. Within computational pathology, pathomics (the extraction of handcrafted, high-dimensional features from digitized histological images) and deep learning (DL)-based whole-slide image analysis have been investigated for the prediction of molecular subtypes, biomarker expression, tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, and treatment response in TNBC. AI models, including DL and multimodal systems integrating histopathology, omics, and clinical data, are being explored for patient stratification, risk assessment, and therapy personalization, encompassing chemotherapy, immunotherapy, PARP inhibitors, and antibody-drug conjugates. By linking spatial tissue architecture with molecular profiles, these approaches may provide new insights into tumor biology and the tumor microenvironment. Most TNBC-specific studies are retrospective, small or single-center, few have been externally validated and, to our knowledge, none has yet demonstrated clinical utility in prospective trials; prediction of biomarkers such as PD-L1 or homologous recombination deficiency from hematoxylin and eosin slides remains investigational and cannot replace validated testing. Despite these challenges, AI-assisted computational pathology is a promising decision-support tool, which complements and does not replace pathologists and oncologists, for enhancing diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic decision-making in TNBC.

W7225297822.abstract: Artificial intelligence-based agents are emerging as a transformative paradigm for agriculture, enabling autonomous perception, reasoning, decision-making, and coordinated action across complex data and operational environments. These systems could improve productivity, resilience, resource efficiency, and food security, while raising challenges related to robustness, interoperability, data governance, trust, equity, and regulation. This Review examines the rise of these systems in agriculture and outlines research priorities for their development and deployment.

W7225343535.abstract: ABSTRACT Garnet‐type solid‐state electrolytes (SSEs) are widely regarded as key materials for high‐energy lithium‐ion solid‐state batteries (LSSBs), owing to their compatibility with lithium metal anodes and high‐voltage cathodes. However, their practical application is limited by multiscale degradation processes, including interfacial instability, space‐charge‐layer formation, surface contamination, structural defects, and electro‐chemo‐mechanical lithium penetration. Revealing the dynamic evolution of these failure mechanisms and the associated interfacial reaction and ion transport processes is essential for developing high‐performance LSSBs. Advanced characterization techniques serve as powerful tools to unravel the complex physicochemical processes occurring in SSEs and at electrode/electrolyte interfaces. Herein, we review recent research advances in spectroscopic, microscopic, scattering, and operando methods for characterizing dynamic processes in SSEs, aiming to provide mechanistic insights into interfacial evolution and failure mechanisms related to lithium penetration. Furthermore, it is demonstrated how such characterization‐enabled understanding informs rational design strategies to enhance interfacial stability and suppress dendrite formation, including surface chemical regulation and microstructural engineering, and how the effectiveness of these approaches is validated by electrochemical characterization. Deeper insights into the microstructure and mechanisms of SSEs are still limited by spatial and temporal resolution, making it difficult to elucidate the evolution of buried interfaces. Finally, future perspectives are outlined, highlighting multimodal operando characterization, quantitative structure–property correlations, machine learning‐assisted analysis, and artificial intelligence‐driven materials discovery for next‐generation garnet‐type LSSBs.

W7225394576.abstract: Cancer is a significant global health issue. Early detection is key for improving treatment outcomes and increasing survival rates. Tissue biopsies provide useful histological and molecular information; however they are an invasive and may not accurately reflect the heterogeneous nature of tumours. Non-invasive methods are therefore being developed. Liquid biopsy allows tumour biomarkers to be analysed from bodily fluids such as blood. Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA), circulating tumour cells (CTCs), extracellular vesicles (EVs) and cell-free RNA (cfRNA) are all biomarkers that can be found in liquid biopsies. Recent developments in technology such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), next-generation sequencing (NGS), DNA methylation, microfluidics, biosensors, nanotechnology and artificial intelligence (AI) have increased the use of liquid biopsies. They can now be used to aid cancer profiling, monitor response to treatment, identify minimal residual disease and detect cancer recurrence. There are several challenges within liquid biopsies, including low biomarker concentrations, variability between samples, interference from clonal haematopoiesis, high costs of testing and limited clinical validation. This review outlines the main biomarkers used for liquid biopsies, new technologies emerging to detect them, their uses in the clinic, limitations with liquid biopsies and future research. Technological advancements and large clinical validation will be key in making liquid biopsies a reliable tool for personalising cancer management.
